title: Mirabel and the Cellar
premise: Orsen Blackwood, a cynical late-night radio host, begins receiving calls from listeners who died the previous week — and when he dismisses them on air, an old wooden chair appears in every photograph taken inside his grandmother Mirabel's house. The chair is a seat being reserved for him by something in the cellar that keeps a count of the family's debts. As Orsen investigates his family's buried history — a lynching his great-grandfather orchestrated and a girl who was never mourned — he realizes the entity is not hunting randomly but collecting justice the law never delivered. To save his family, Orsen must choose between exposing the truth that will destroy the Blackwood name or taking the reserved seat himself; in the end he confesses everything live on air, and the cellar takes him instead of the innocent.
about_author: Lena Delacroix is the pen name of a former small-town radio producer who spent years reading obituaries on air before turning to horror fiction. She writes from a farmhouse in upstate New York that she insists has no cellar.

chapters.title: The Dead Call In
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. During his late-night show, a caller describes her own funeral in detail; Orsen assumes a prank until the voice matches a woman whose obituary ran that morning. The beat is uneasy skepticism — he laughs it off on air, but his hands shake during the break.

chapters.title: Grandma's House Has One More Chair
chapters.summary: Orsen visits Mirabel's house to help her sort photos for her eightieth birthday. Every picture now includes a plain wooden chair that wasn't there before, always empty, always facing the camera. POV alternates Orsen and Mirabel. Emotional beat: creeping wrongness beneath family warmth.

chapters.title: Second Caller, Same Week
chapters.summary: A man calls claiming to be Orsen's childhood friend Danny — dead six days. He warns Orsen: 'Stop counting the chairs.' Orsen pulls the station's call logs and finds no record of either call. His denial hardens into obsession. Beat: rational mind cracking.

chapters.title: The Cellar Door
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She remembers the cellar was sealed in 1961 after her brother's disappearance, yet finds it open, cold air rising, and hears a slow rhythmic knocking like someone keeping time. She tells no one. Beat: dread and complicity — she knows more than she says.

chapters.title: Family Reunion, Minus One
chapters.summary: The Blackwoods gather for Mirabel's birthday. Cousin Ruth photographs everything; later, in every image, the extra chair sits at the table's head. Aunt Carol counts aloud and goes pale. Orsen's POV. Beat: the horror becomes communal, undeniable.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Says
chapters.summary: Searching Mirabel's attic, Orsen finds a ledger from 1932 listing names crossed out one by one — the last entry unfinished: 'E. Vane.' His great-grandfather Aldous Blackwood's handwriting. Beat: the past is a debt register, and the family are debtors.

chapters.title: Mirabel Confesses Half
chapters.summary: Mirabel admits Aldous led a mob against a young woman, Etta Vane, accused unjustly; she vanished into the cellar and was never found. But Mirabel refuses to say what happened afterward. Orsen's POV. Beat: loyalty vs. truth — love for grandma versus the need to know.

chapters.title: The Count Begins
chapters.summary: Aunt Carol dies suddenly in her sleep; the next morning her photo shows the chair occupied by a faint silhouette. A new photograph appears on the fridge, unbidden: the chair moved one place closer to Orsen. Beat: grief weaponized as countdown.

chapters.title: On Air, Off Record
chapters.summary: Orsen devotes his show to Etta Vane, asking listeners for information. A caller whispers directions to the house where Etta lived — then says, 'She's still down there. She wants a verdict.' Beat: Orsen stops denying and starts investigating.

chapters.title: Ruth Runs
chapters.summary: Ruth, terrified, flees town with her kids; her car is found idling on the county line, doors open, everyone gone — except their phones, which keep sending photos of the chair. Orsen's POV, guilt-ridden. Beat: escape is impossible; the count follows blood.

chapters.title: Down the Stairs
chapters.summary: Orsen enters the cellar despite Mirabel's pleas. It is larger than the house above, walls papered with decades of missing-person flyers, all Blackwood relatives. At the center: the chair, and a shallow depression in the floor shaped like a body. Beat: confrontation with the physical truth.

chapters.title: Etta
chapters.summary: In the cellar dark, Orsen meets Etta — or what remains of her, patient and terrible. She doesn't threaten; she asks him to say her name correctly, to say what Aldous did. He flees instead. Beat: shame; the monster only wants acknowledgment.

chapters.title: The Station Goes Silent
chapters.summary: Orsen tries to broadcast Etta's story; the FCC shuts the frequency citing interference, and his producer quits, whispering that Orsen 'sounds like them now.' Isolated, he records a confession alone in the studio. Beat: institutions fail; truth must be carried personally.

chapters.title: Mirabel's Whole Truth
chapters.summary: Mirabel finally reveals she was a child in the house in 1932 — she heard Etta in the cellar for three days and did nothing, told no one, because Aldous made her promise. Her silence sealed the haunting. Beat: devastating; loyalty was the original sin.

chapters.title: Two Seats Left
chapters.summary: The photographs update: the chair now sits beside Orsen's, and a second chair appears facing Mirabel. The count is nearly complete. Orsen realizes the entity isn't vengeful — it's procedural, waiting for a lawful verdict no court ever gave. Beat: grim clarity.

chapters.title: The Trial in the Kitchen
chapters.summary: Orsen convenes the surviving family and holds a mock trial over the kitchen table, reading the ledger aloud, entering evidence, letting Mirabel testify. Etta manifests as a listener calling in on the kitchen radio. Beat: justice outside the law, fragile and human.

chapters.title: Verdict, Overturned
chapters.summary: The family votes to declare Etta innocent — but the chairs don't move. Etta's voice through the radio: innocence acknowledged isn't enough; someone must serve the sentence Aldous escaped. Beat: horror of incomplete absolution; the climax looms.

chapters.title: Orsen's Broadcast
chapters.summary: Orsen hijacks his own show one final time, confessing the family crime live, naming every victim, playing the ledger page on air so thousands hear it. The switchboard lights with the dead, all saying thank you. Beat: catharsis and sacrifice chosen freely.

chapters.title: The Seat Reserved
chapters.summary: That night the cellar door stands open and the chair waits at its foot. Orsen says goodbye to Mirabel, who begs to take his place; he refuses — the debt is his name's to pay. Beat: love expressed through self-sacrifice; loyalty fulfilled at last.

chapters.title: Descent
chapters.summary: Orsen descends and sits in the chair. Etta appears whole for the first time, and the cellar fills with light like a courtroom at dawn. The flyers peel from the walls. He speaks her eulogy as the floor closes gently over him. Beat: terrifying peace; climax resolved.

chapters.title: After the Count
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The photographs lose the chair; the calls stop; Ruth and the children return, remembering nothing. Mirabel keeps one photo — Orsen seated, smiling faintly, at peace. Beat: mourning without closure, identity reshaped by inherited guilt.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Epilogue, mixed POV. Months later, a new host takes the midnight slot. At 3:03 a.m., a calm voice calls in and says, 'This is Orsen Blackwood. I'd like to request a song for my grandmother.' The host plays it. Beat: bittersweet resonance — some voices the dead keep.
